title: Correction: SETD1B mutations confer apoptosis resistance and BCL2 independence in B cell lymphoma.
Survivin Promotes the Formation of a Microtubule-Based Glycolytic Hub
summary: KRAS is one of the most frequently mutated oncoproteins in cancer. Its ability to induce malignant transformation relies on metabolic reprogramming that causes cells to become dependent on aerobic glycolysis as a primary source of energy and for generating biological building blocks. Thus far, the signaling mechanism used by oncogenic KRAS to promote these changes in cancer cell metabolism has not been fully elucidated. However, through studies in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell lines and patient-derived organoids, we now demonstrate how oncogenic KRAS triggers an increase in glycolytic activity and identify Survivin as a newly discovered and critical KRAS-signaling partner essential for promoting these metabolic changes. We show that oncogenic KRAS potently upregulates the expression of Survivin in PDAC cells and patient-derived organoids undergoing increased glycolysis, whereas depleting Survivin expression inhibits their glycolytic activity and growth. Through a combination of cellular, biochemical, and imaging approaches, we further show that Survivin promotes the formation of unique microtubule-based structures that resemble invadosome rosettes, allowing for the recruitment of the glycolytic enzymes triose phosphate isomerase (TPI) and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) to these super-structures which drives the increases in glycolysis. These findings demonstrate that by directing the assembly of a microtubule-based complex of metabolic enzymes, Survivin serves as a vital link in a KRAS signaling pathway responsible for promoting the metabolic changes necessary for the accelerated growth of PDAC cells, and thus potentially highlight new therapeutic strategies for treating KRAS-dependent cancers.

title: Metabolic engineering of Yarrowia lipolytica for higher fatty alcohol production
summary: Fatty alcohols are versatile chemicals with growing demand across a broad range of industries, yet conventional production methods pose environmental challenges. Microbial biosynthesis offers a promising alternative, if hosts can be engineered to achieve high product titers. The industrially relevant oleaginous yeast Yarrowia lipolytica is well suited to this challenge because of its natural capacity for lipid metabolism. Here, we engineered Y. lipolytica W29 for fatty alcohol production by disrupting pathways involved in lipogenesis and fatty alcohol oxidation, identifying fatty alcohol oxidation as a major constraint on product accumulation. Initial engineering yielded fatty alcohol titers of 2.5 g/L from 40 g/L glucose. Subsequent optimization of media supplements and nutrient concentrations, combined with deletion of the citrate transporter CEX1 and addition of 1% Tergitol to the extractive culture medium, increased titers to 10.9 g/L in shake flasks with 80 g/L glucose and a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of 60. Scaling the process to fed-batch bioreactor cultivation further increased titers to 19.4 g/L. These results demonstrate that combining metabolic engineering with medium and process optimization enables high-titer fatty alcohol production in Y. lipolytica.

title: The Sensitivity of 13C-Metabolic Flux Analysis to Biomass Composition Underscores the Need for Accurate Biomass Formulation in Escherichia coli
summary: Quantifying intracellular fluxes through 13C-metabolic flux analysis (13C-MFA) provides a detailed view of cellular metabolism. While model formulation, including biomass synthesis reactions, is known to influence flux estimations, the degree to which biomass composition affects 13C-MFA outcomes in Escherichia coli remains debated. Here, we reconstructed a genome-scale 13C-MFA model of E. coli incorporating explicit nucleotide biosynthesis and a modular biomass formulation that separates protein, RNA, and other components. Using isotopic labeling experiments and systematic perturbations of biomass composition, we demonstrate that 13C-MFA can robustly differentiate subtle shifts in the protein/RNA ratio, with deviations as small as 2-3% producing statistically significant but biologically interpretable changes in model fit. Reaction-level analyses revealed consistent flux adjustments across amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis, while pathways in one-carbon metabolism, particularly serine, glycine, and threonine interconversions, exhibited the strongest responses. Collectively, these results highlight the robustness and discriminative power of 13C-MFA and also demonstrate the importance of accurate biomass composition measurement in E. coli 13C-MFA, given the intrinsic sensitivity of the method to macromolecular stoichiometry.

title: Advanced Maternal Age Impairs Decidual Angiogenesis and Spiral Artery Remodelling
summary: Pregnancy presents an extreme physiological challenge that relies on rapid angiogenic vascular expansion and remodelling to establish the maternal-fetal vascular unit at the uteroplacental interface. These adaptations to the pregnancy-specific decidual vasculature are necessary for pregnancy progression. Advanced age pregnancies (AAP; pregnant person >35 years old) are associated with increased risk of poor pregnancy outcomes. Despite increasing evidence of the centrality of vascular aging in mediating organotypic dysfunction, whether vascular aging in the decidua occurs in the context of AAP is unknown. Using a murine model of AAP, we find that alongside embryonic developmental delay and deficient placental vascularization, AAP dams had impaired decidual angiogenesis and spiral artery remodeling with imbalances in both systemic and local uterine angiogenic factor expression in the VEGF and angiopoietin signalling families. These findings reveal that pregnancy may expose vascular aging mechanisms that contribute to declining reproductive success and increased cardiovascular risk later in life.

title: Elucidating changes in gene expression driving nuclear dynamics across a foraminiferal life cycle with Pheno2Seq
summary: In many microeukaryotes, conserved morphology masks transitions between haploid and diploid phases of the life cycle, making it difficult to link gene expression to development. Hence, insights on such transitions come largely from model lineages of animals, plants and fungi. To address this gap, we developed a method, Pheno2Seq, that enables visualization of fluorescently-stained individuals followed by identification of candidate genes through single-cell transcriptome analyses. We applied this method in Allogromia laticollaris, a foraminifera with a complex life cycle that alternates between haploid and diploid phases and includes endoreplication to ~11,000N. As this taxon lacks a reference genome, we used a conservative phylogenomic approach to identify gene families present across diverse foraminifera. We identified >800 differentially expressed genes underlying life cycle transitions along with a similar number of constitutively-expressed genes. During Zerfall, a phase of extreme endoreplication, the transcriptome is largely silenced with the exception of gene families involved in genome processes and stability. Intriguingly, these gene families include chromatin modifiers, spliceosomal components and histone paralogs, some of which are known to contribute to cell type differentiation in multicellular eukaryotes. We also find numerous genes involved in DNA repair (e.g. DNA damage response and R-loop regulating genes). We speculate that these genes are part of an ancient eukaryotic toolkit, likely present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) and that regulates genomes during life cycle transitions. Our method, Pheno2Seq, can be adapted to diverse lineages to enable the study of life cycle regulation in microeukaryotes that lack morphologically distinguishable life cycle stages.
